title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
authors: Julian Brandon, Bruno Loureiro, N Alex Cayco-Gajic, Arthur Pellegrino
abstract: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.

infographic.key_insight: Learning dynamics in dynamical systems-based generative models can favor low-rank representations, linking feature learning to persistent or training-budget-dependent mode collapse.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Generative-model training may miss smaller modes because collapse is stable or those modes require longer to learn.
method: Express gradient flow for a general class of stochastic differential equations as compositions of linear operators.
Relate operator structure to low-rank biases and collapse.
Study stable collapsed solutions and sequential feature learning in variational inference and flow matching.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports two collapse mechanisms in variational inference and flow-matching tasks, but provides no datasets, quantitative metrics, or benchmark comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish how broadly these mechanisms predict collapse in practical, large-scale generative models.
infographic.paper_title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models

title: Deep backward multistep high-order regression methods for high dimensional nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations
authors: Qiang Han, Shaolin Ji, Zihao Xv
abstract: We propose a deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) method for semilinear parabolic partial differential equations through their backward stochastic differential equation representations. The method combines multistep time discretization with regression targets formed by conditional expectations. Under explicit regularity, starting-value, forward-approximation and network-moment assumptions, we prove an error bound separating time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling and neural-network approximation. The analysis assumes exact population minimization; finite-training-sample generalization and optimization errors are not included. For generators independent of the gradient variable, suitably constrained GroupSort networks and sufficiently large conditional sample sizes give order $J$ in the stated nodal $L^2$ error norm. The required network sizes depend on dimension, so this result does not establish dimension-independent complexity. We present a reproducible time-discretization test satisfying the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks, whose relation to the assumptions is discussed explicitly.

infographic.key_insight: Deep backward multistep high-order regression (MHDBR) combines BSDE representations and neural regression to solve high-dimensional semilinear parabolic PDEs with a decomposed error bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a framework for balancing time discretization, conditional Monte Carlo sampling, and network approximation in high-dimensional PDE solvers.
method: Represent the PDE through a backward stochastic differential equation.
Combine multistep time discretization with conditional-expectation regression targets.
For gradient-independent generators, obtain order J in nodal L² error using constrained GroupSort networks and sufficiently large conditional samples.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation includes a reproducible time-discretization test satisfying the analytical assumptions and three broader neural-network benchmarks whose alignment with those assumptions is discussed.
infographic.watch_item: The theory assumes exact population minimization, excludes finite-training-sample generalization and optimization errors, and does not establish dimension-independent complexity.
infographic.paper_title: Deep backward multistep high-order regression methods for high dimensional nonlinear parabolic partial differential equations

title: BiMuon: A Geometry-Aware Stochastic Bilevel Optimization Approach
authors: Zhen Qin, Zhiyao Zhang, Yingbin Liang, Jia Liu
abstract: Stochastic bilevel optimization provides a general framework for many machine learning applications, such as hyperparameter learning, data reweighting, language model alignment, and actor-critic reinforcement learning. However, most existing bilevel optimization methods treat matrix-valued gradients as flattened vectors and perform optimization in the resulting vectorized space, ignoring the matrix structures common in modern neural networks. Moreover, the lower-level (LL) problem curvature can induce significant spectral imbalance in the upper-level (UL) geometry. Such limitations of existing bilevel optimization methods motivate us to develop BiMuon, a geometry-aware stochastic bilevel optimization method that integrates implicit hypergradient estimation in bilevel optimization with Muon-style orthogonalized updates at the UL. To our knowledge, BiMuon is the first stochastic BLO method with Muon-style orthogonalized matrix updates and an $O(ε^{-4})$ iteration-complexity guarantee, matching the best-known rates achieved by Muon-type methods based on matrix parameterizations. To improve computational and parallel efficiency for models with multiple matrix parameters, we further study BiMuon for blockwise diagonal matrix approximation and derive a relative stepsize allocation rule based on UL progress and blockwise LL sensitivity. We evaluate BiMuon on representation learning and blockwise bilevel optimization, providing empirical support for our methods.

infographic.key_insight: BiMuon preserves matrix structure in stochastic bilevel optimization by combining implicit hypergradient estimation with Muon-style orthogonalized upper-level updates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets matrix-valued learning problems where lower-level curvature can create spectral imbalance in upper-level optimization.
method: Estimate upper-level hypergradients implicitly through the lower-level problem.
Apply Muon-style orthogonalized matrix updates with an O(ε⁻⁴) iteration-complexity guarantee.
Use a block-diagonal approximation and allocate relative step sizes by upper-level progress and blockwise lower-level sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on representation learning and blockwise bilevel optimization provide empirical support, but the abstract reports no quantitative gains.
infographic.watch_item: Practical benefits should be weighed against hypergradient estimation and orthogonalization costs; block-diagonal approximations may miss cross-block interactions.
infographic.paper_title: BiMuon: A Geometry-Aware Stochastic Bilevel Optimization Approach

title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
authors: Rui Zou, Xin Zhao, Mengqi Wei, Ji-Rong Wen
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

infographic.key_insight: BiVerify improves mathematical self-correction by requiring the same candidate solution to pass both backward constraint checks and forward reasoning checks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pairing complementary verification directions can make LLM-based mathematical workflows more reliable than relying on either direction alone.
method: Start with backward verification against the original problem constraints, then check reasoning and objective completeness forward.
Dynamically switch directions, reset verification state, and revise candidates or verification flow based on outcomes.
Use shared mathematical tools to separate logical reasoning from precise computation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five challenging math benchmarks and multiple DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models, BiVerify reports a 13.5-percentage-point average accuracy gain over the strongest representative public baseline evaluated, reaching 31.2 points on GPT.
infographic.watch_item: Repeated verification and revision may add latency and computation cost; the abstract does not quantify this overhead.
infographic.paper_title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction

title: Zeroth-Order Riemannian Optimization on Fixed-Rank Manifolds for LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Xinjue Wang, Xiuheng Wang, Yejun Zhang, Sergiy A. Vorobyov, Esa Ollila
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

infographic.key_insight: Constraining LLM weight updates to fixed-rank matrix manifolds enables gradient-free fine-tuning while preserving the update rank throughout training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach avoids backpropagation activation storage and keeps pretrained weights frozen, offering a memory-efficient fine-tuning strategy.
method: Project random matrices onto the fixed-rank manifold’s tangent space.
Normalize projected directions to correct scale mismatch in the zeroth-order gradient estimator.
Optimize with Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) or its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S.
infographic.evidence_signal: LLM fine-tuning experiments across model families and tasks show competitive performance against strong forward-only baselines, with gains in several settings.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence relies on trajectory-regularity conditions, and the abstract does not quantify practical memory or runtime savings.
infographic.paper_title: Zeroth-Order Riemannian Optimization on Fixed-Rank Manifolds for LLM Fine-Tuning

title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization
authors: Zhiwei Zhai, Xinyu Wang, Wenjing Yan, Lei Ding, Ying-Jun Angela Zhang
abstract: Single-loop minimax methods are appealing for modern machine learning, but standard stochastic gradient updates can be unstable and oscillatory under tightly coupled primal-dual dynamics, making performance notoriously sensitive to stepsizes. To fundamentally improve stability, we develop an orthogonal update framework tailored to minimax optimization, which applies updates along orthogonalized directions to reduce update anisotropy. However, orthogonalization reshapes the optimization geometry and makes coordinating primal-dual stepsizes even more delicate. To overcome this challenge, we develop AdaSGDA, which equips orthogonal updates with an adaptive stepsize rule driven by accumulated gradient norms. This mechanism automatically balances coupled primal-dual progress under orthogonalization, yielding an effectively parameter-free method for nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization. We prove that AdaSGDA avoids problem-dependent tuning while attaining the state-of-the-art $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/4}\right)$ convergence rate. We further propose AdaSGDA-VR, which incorporates a carefully designed variance reduction scheme and achieves the faster $\mathcal{O}\left(T^{-1/3}\right)$ rate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods deliver competitive performance compared to existing minimax optimization methods.

infographic.key_insight: Orthogonal updates paired with gradient-norm-based adaptive stepsizes stabilize coupled minimax optimization while avoiding problem-dependent stepsize tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For machine-learning systems formulated as minimax problems, the framework offers a way to reduce update instability and stepsize sensitivity.
method: Orthogonalize update directions to reduce update anisotropy.
Use AdaSGDA to adapt primal-dual stepsizes from accumulated gradient norms.
Add variance reduction in AdaSGDA-VR to improve the convergence rate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence rates of O(T^−1/4) for AdaSGDA and O(T^−1/3) for AdaSGDA-VR, plus extensive experiments showing competitive performance without specifying benchmarks or numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: The stated guarantees target nonconvex–strongly-concave problems; applicability beyond that setting and implementation overhead require evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Orthogonal Updates for the Win: Towards Accelerated Adaptive Minimax Optimization

title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds
authors: Vitalii Aksenov, Sebastian Gutierrez Hernandez
abstract: We propose a fixed-point acceleration method for optimization over probability measures, applicable to a variety of machine learning problems. We represent probability measures as pushforwards of a reference distribution through a neural network map and equip the parameter space with the induced pullback Wasserstein metric. This geometric structure allows natural gradient descent to be interpreted as a fixed-point iteration on a Riemannian manifold. We accelerate this iteration using Riemannian Anderson mixing method, which exploits historical residuals to capture approximate second-order information without forming Hessians. In the present parametric setting, the manifold is represented by Euclidean coordinates endowed with a point-dependent metric, simplifying retraction and vector transport. We evaluate the method on multimodal sampling, PDE-based inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling. Across the tested tasks, Anderson mixing reduces the number of natural-gradient iterations and achieves competitive performance relative to SGD and Adam in terms of both loss-gradient evaluations and wall-clock time. These results suggest that fixed-point acceleration is an efficient tool for improving the computational efficiency of training on parametric Wasserstein methods.

infographic.key_insight: Riemannian Anderson mixing accelerates natural-gradient optimization of neural probability measures by using past residuals to approximate second-order information without forming Hessians.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can reduce optimization effort in sampling, inverse problems, and generative modeling built on neural Wasserstein geometry.
method: Represent probability measures as neural-network pushforwards of a reference distribution.
Equip network parameters with a pullback Wasserstein metric and interpret natural-gradient descent as a manifold fixed-point iteration.
Accelerate updates with Riemannian Anderson mixing using historical residuals.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multimodal sampling, PDE inverse problems, aggregation dynamics, Bayesian logistic regression, and generative modeling, the abstract reports fewer natural-gradient iterations and competitive gradient-evaluation counts and wall-clock time versus SGD and Adam.
infographic.watch_item: Practical speedups may depend on the cost and numerical stability of computations involving the parameter-dependent Wasserstein metric.
infographic.paper_title: Fixed-point acceleration on Neural Wasserstein manifolds

title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models
authors: Yibo Miao, Yichuan Cao, Xiao-Shan Gao, Yinpeng Dong
abstract: LLMs are powerful but incur substantial inference cost, which can be exploited by malicious users to induce overly long outputs, increasing latency and operational expense. Prior resource consumption attacks either coerce repetition or suppress the end-of-sequence token by lowering its logit value. However, with autoregressive, sampling-based generation, the search space grows exponentially with length and small deviations or unstable trajectories can derail optimization, limiting attack effectiveness and stability. To address this issue, we introduce Chatter Attack, a novel class of resource consumption attacks that optimize adversarial prompts to induce predefined short target phrases, thereby avoiding search-space explosion while still eliciting long responses. Specifically, Chatter Attack triggers self-doubt using short doubt-inducing phrases as the target, and sustains this state throughout generation via inference attention loss and global entropy loss. To extend to black-box settings, we further propose a novel Bayesian Prompt Optimization (BPO) method, which models the objective function globally by constructing a discrete token kernel, efficiently exploring the entire search space using prior information. Extensive experiments across multiple models and datasets show that our method outperforms baselines, with maximum response length increases to 31.5$\times$, and revealing practical resource-depletion risks for real-world LLM inference services.

infographic.key_insight: Chatter Attack induces prolonged LLM responses by targeting short, doubt-inducing phrases rather than directly optimizing long output sequences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The attack exposes a resource-depletion risk for LLM inference services through increased generation latency and operational cost.
method: Optimize adversarial prompts to elicit predefined short phrases that trigger self-doubt.
Use inference attention loss and global entropy loss to sustain this behavior during generation.
Extend to black-box settings with Bayesian Prompt Optimization using a discrete token kernel.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluations across multiple models and datasets, outperforming baselines with response-length increases of up to 31.5×.
infographic.watch_item: The 31.5× figure is a reported maximum; the abstract does not specify typical gains, attack-query costs, or effectiveness under output limits.
infographic.paper_title: Chatter Attack: Resource Consumption Attack for Large Language Models

title: Total variation error bounds for Schrödinger-Föllmer samplers
authors: Xiaojie Wang, Xiaoyan Zhang
abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional, multimodal target distributions plays a fundamental role in scientific computing, statistics and machine learning. Recently, the Schrödinger-Föllmer sampler (SFS) has been proposed by Huang et al. (IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory, 2025) as an efficient sampling algorithm that transports the degenerate distribution at $t=0$ to the target distribution at $t=1$, without relying on long-time ergodicity. In this paper, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds for SFS in the total variation distance by deriving regularization estimates for the associated Kolmogorov equation via the Bismut-Elworthy-Li formula. When the drift can be computed exactly, a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}( h|\ln h|)$ was obtained under certain smoothness conditions on the drift with a uniform time step-size $h>0$. When the drift is approximated by Monte Carlo methods, we obtain a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}( h|\ln h|+ 1/M)$, where $M$ is the number of samples used in the Monte Carlo approximation. This yields a sharper dependence on $M$ than the existing bound $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{M})$ in the $L^2$-Wasserstein distance in the aforementioned paper, by turning the total variation error to the weak error analysis in the setting of non-smooth test functions. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the convergence rate with respect to the time step-size $h$ and the Monte Carlo sample size $M$ and the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

infographic.key_insight: Under drift smoothness assumptions, Schrödinger–Föllmer samplers achieve total variation error bounds of O(h|ln h|) with exact drift and O(h|ln h| + 1/M) with Monte Carlo drift estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These finite-time guarantees help guide time-step and Monte Carlo sample-budget choices for high-dimensional, multimodal sampling without relying on long-time ergodicity.
method: Analyze transport from a point mass at t=0 to the target distribution at t=1.
Use the Bismut–Elworthy–Li formula to derive Kolmogorov-equation regularization estimates.
Bound total variation error through weak-error analysis with non-smooth test functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments illustrate convergence with respect to time-step size h and Monte Carlo sample count M, alongside sampler effectiveness.
infographic.watch_item: The bounds require regularity assumptions; the improved 1/M dependence is measured in total variation, unlike the earlier 1/√M bound in L²-Wasserstein distance.
infographic.paper_title: Total variation error bounds for Schrödinger-Föllmer samplers

title: On the Global Convergence of Stochastic Adam for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Yihang Gao
abstract: The Adam optimizer is widely used to train neural networks with highly nonlinear and nonconvex objective functions. Remarkably, Adam often drives the empirical training loss nearly to zero. This phenomenon has been partially explained by neural tangent kernel (NTK) analyses of gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, analyzing Adam presents additional challenges. Its first-moment momentum couples stochastic gradients across iterations, while its adaptive second-moment preconditioner depends on the same stochastic gradient used in the update. In this paper, we establish linear convergence guarantees for Adam in training sufficiently wide two-layer neural networks with either full-batch or minibatch gradients. For full-batch Adam, we construct a Lyapunov function to control the effect of historical momentum. For minibatch Adam, our analysis builds on an exact virtual-iterate representation, a conditional analysis of the dependence between stochastic gradients and adaptive preconditioners, and uniform concentration bounds for the second-moment estimates. We prove geometric decay of the empirical loss for full-batch Adam and geometric decay in restricted expectation on a high-probability event for minibatch Adam. Beyond regression, we extend our convergence analysis to physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for solving the Poisson equation, where differential operators and separate sampling of interior and boundary points introduce additional challenges. We establish analogous global convergence guarantees for both deterministic and stochastic Adam under explicit conditions on network width and Adam's parameters, characterizing the effects of minibatch size on convergence. These results help bridge the gap between Adam's empirical success and its theoretical understanding, providing sharper convergence guarantees for PINNs than existing analyses.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proves global linear convergence of full-batch and minibatch Adam for sufficiently wide two-layer networks, including physics-informed networks solving the Poisson equation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide theoretical guidance on how network width, Adam parameters, and minibatch size affect reliable loss reduction in PINN training.
method: Construct a Lyapunov function to control full-batch Adam’s momentum history.
Analyze minibatch Adam using exact virtual iterates, gradient–preconditioner dependence, and second-moment concentration bounds.
Extend convergence guarantees to Poisson PINNs with separately sampled interior and boundary points.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical geometric loss-decay guarantees, with minibatch results in restricted expectation on a high-probability event; no empirical benchmarks are described.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees require sufficiently wide two-layer networks and explicit parameter conditions, so they do not automatically extend to practical deep PINNs or other PDEs.
infographic.paper_title: On the Global Convergence of Stochastic Adam for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence
authors: Baiyu Su, Lizhang Chen, Qiang Liu
abstract: AdamW is ubiquitous in deep learning, yet its behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze its dynamics through the lens of dynamical systems and show that AdamW admits an implicit fixed-point objective: its fixed points coincide with the stationary points of a constrained and regularized optimization problem. However, not all of these fixed points are stable under AdamW's dynamics, and stability depends sensitively on curvature, weight decay, and momentum parameters. Even in one-dimensional settings, equilibria may be unstable, and trajectories can exhibit persistent oscillations rather than convergence to them. We further extend the analysis to higher dimensions, deriving sufficient conditions for local stability of the continuous-time dynamics, and propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW's fixed points. These results clarify what optimization problem AdamW is associated with, when its convergence can be expected, and how its dynamics could inspire more reliable optimizers.

infographic.key_insight: AdamW’s fixed points match stationary points of an implicit constrained, regularized objective, but some are unstable and need not attract its trajectories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable use of AdamW requires attention to curvature, weight decay, and momentum, which can affect stability even near stationary points.
method: Characterize AdamW’s fixed points through an implicit optimization objective.
Analyze one-dimensional instability and derive sufficient local stability conditions for higher-dimensional continuous-time dynamics.
Propose a convergent modification that preserves AdamW’s fixed points.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical stability results and persistent oscillations even in one dimension, but provides no dataset benchmarks or quantitative evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Higher-dimensional continuous-time local stability conditions do not by themselves guarantee convergence of practical discrete-time AdamW.
infographic.paper_title: A Stability Analysis of AdamW: Unstable Equilibria and Non-Convergence

title: DisMUSE: An Efficient Distributed Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization Approach with Theoretical Convergence Guarantee
authors: Zhen Qin, Zhiyao Zhang, Yingbin Liang, Jia Liu
abstract: In recent years, singular-spectrum-based optimizers have attracted increasing attention due to their ability to preserve the matrix structure of neural network gradients, thereby enabling geometry-aware optimization. However, most singular-spectrum-based (SSB) approaches remain centralized, limiting their use in distributed learning infrastructures that exploit massive parallelism. Distributed SSB optimization is still at an early stage, with open questions about convergence guarantees and communication efficiency. To fill this gap, we propose the Distributed Momentum-based Spectral Estimator (DisMUSE), an efficient distributed SSB optimization framework for both data-center and federated settings. Using Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum as the spectral update, DisMUSE integrates a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator and achieves an $O((KT)^{-1/3})$ convergence rate, where $K$ and $T$ denote the number of nodes and local iterations per node, respectively. This rate matches the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization. Building on this variance-reduced framework, we study two extensions. First, our DisMUSE method with finite Newton-Schulz (NS) iterations preserves the same convergence order under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, up to a multiplicative factor. Second, we develop a communication-efficient variant based on low-rank (LR) momentum transmission and quantify the error it introduces to the stationarity bound, characterizing the trade-off between accuracy and communication cost.

infographic.key_insight: DisMUSE brings geometry-aware, singular-spectrum-based optimization to distributed learning with a theoretical O((KT)^(-1/3)) convergence rate, where K is the node count and T is local iterations per node.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets data-center and federated training, offering spectral updates with explicit accuracy–communication trade-offs.
method: Combine Muon-style exact orthogonalized momentum with a recursive variance-reduced momentum estimator.
Approximate spectral updates using finite Newton–Schulz iterations.
Reduce communication through low-rank momentum transmission.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence matching the best-known rates for variance-reduced nonconvex distributed optimization, but provides no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Finite Newton–Schulz updates retain the convergence order only under a uniform normalized support-spectrum condition, while low-rank transmission introduces stationarity error.
infographic.paper_title: DisMUSE: An Efficient Distributed Singular-Spectrum-Based Optimization Approach with Theoretical Convergence Guarantee

title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions
authors: Guneykan Ozgul, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shree Hari Sureshbabu, Shouvanik Chakrabarti
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a workhorse algorithm for continuous optimization. It is a folk belief among deep learning practitioners that learning rate decay in SGD substantially improves performance. However, it has remained unclear whether learning rate decay offers an asymptotic advantage for global nonconvex optimization. We answer this question in the affirmative by demonstrating a natural class of nonconvex functions for which, we prove that SGD with learning rate decay requires exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step size regime. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exponential advantage that has been demonstrated for learning rate decay. The class of functions we consider includes many popular benchmark nonconvex functions. Our results provide a robust explanatory theory for the empirically observed benefits of learning rate decay for global optimization. We show that annealing performs the non-logconcave sampling task associated to the optimization problem in polynomial time, via a novel application of weak Poincaré inequalities.

infographic.key_insight: For a natural class of nonconvex functions, SGD with learning rate decay provably needs exponentially fewer gradient queries for global optimization than SGD with any fixed learning rate in the small-step-size regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result provides theoretical support for learning rate decay in nonconvex optimization, though it does not establish the same speedup for arbitrary engineering or deep learning objectives.
method: Analyze a nonconvex function class containing many popular benchmark functions.
Compare gradient-query complexity for decaying versus fixed learning rates.
Use weak Poincaré inequalities to prove polynomial-time annealing for the associated non-logconcave sampling task.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical exponential separation, but gives no numerical experiments or empirical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee is restricted to the studied function class and small-step-size regime; practical schedule selection requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Rate Decay Can Exponentially Accelerate SGD for Global Optimization of Nonconvex Functions

title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
authors: Paul Häusner, Jevgenija Rudzusika, Jens Sjölund, Ozan Öktem
abstract: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.

infographic.key_insight: Learned neural subproblem solvers accelerate inexact alternating minimization, with optimality-gap guarantees for convex, quadratically coupled problems satisfying quadratic growth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Replacing costly inner solves with trained networks can reduce runtime in robust matrix completion and dictionary-regularized low-dose CT reconstruction.
method: Use neural networks to approximate alternating subproblem solutions.
Train greedily using per-iteration errors exposed by a worst-case optimality-gap bound.
Combine the bound with PAC-Bayes analysis for a fixed-horizon, high-probability guarantee on the expected gap over problem instances.
infographic.evidence_signal: On robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction, the authors report 5×–13× speedups over an inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy, reaching up to 30× after brief end-to-end fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require the stated convexity, quadratic-coupling, and quadratic-growth assumptions and are fixed-horizon rather than unrestricted convergence guarantees.
infographic.paper_title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling

title: Accelerated Reinforcement Learning for Soft Robotics: Hours Instead of Years
authors: Roshan S. Kaundinya, Hehui Zheng, Robert K. Katzschmann, George Haller
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.

infographic.key_insight: A six-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM) model enables soft-robot reinforcement learning in 3 hours, versus an extrapolated 3 years of hardware interaction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact, data-learned dynamics can accelerate controller training while enabling deployment on nonlinear soft hardware without policy fine-tuning.

Learn a 6,924-parameter polynomial ordinary differential equation from pre-collected data.
Train a trajectory-tracking policy in the reduced simulator and deploy it directly.

infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports one soft-arm platform; transfer to other robots or operating regimes may require new data and validation of the time-scale separation.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerated Reinforcement Learning for Soft Robotics: Hours Instead of Years

title: Learning calibrated probabilistic forecasts using Koopman mode decomposition and the continuous ranked probability score
authors: Benjamin M. Kent, Richard E. Turner
abstract: Well-calibrated forecasting for non-linear dynamical systems is essential in science and engineering applications such as fluid dynamics and weather prediction. We present a forecasting method combining probabilistic machine learning with the structured linear dynamics of Koopman mode decomposition. Within this framework, the observation, linear dynamics, and state reconstruction operators are constructed using standard machine learning architectures, producing predictive distributions via the pushforward of injected noise samples. The model is trained using a proper scoring rule, the continuous ranked probability score, to directly target calibrated, accurate forecasts. The approach is validated on two non-linear ordinary differential equation examples and two partial differential equation examples, vortex shedding and cavity flow, using both large and small, noisy datasets. Results demonstrate that known Koopman eigenfunctions and spectra can be identified and used for accurate forecasting. The model can also produce multi-modal predictive distributions, demonstrated for a trajectory initialised on the boundary between two basins of attraction. Uncertainty is captured by the sample ensemble spread, with spread--skill ratios close to one over the training horizon in several experiments, although for extended rollouts and noisy datasets, the ensemble may become under- or over-dispersed. In low-noise experiments, temporal rollout is generally accurate for at least twice the training horizon, and up to twenty times in some cases. Approximation quality is comparable to a deep ensemble approximation over the training horizon, but at a reduced computational cost and with better robustness in identifying Koopman eigenvalues.

infographic.key_insight: Combining Koopman-structured linear dynamics with probabilistic learning produces accurate forecasts with calibrated uncertainty in several nonlinear-system experiments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a potentially lower-cost alternative to deep ensembles for uncertainty-aware forecasting in applications such as fluid dynamics.
method: Learn observation, linear dynamics, and state reconstruction operators using machine learning architectures.
Push injected noise samples through the model to generate predictive ensembles.
Train with the continuous ranked probability score to target accurate, calibrated forecasts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on two nonlinear ODE systems, vortex shedding, and cavity flow showed spread–skill ratios near one in several experiments and low-noise forecast accuracy extending to 2–20 times the training horizon.
infographic.watch_item: Calibration can degrade during extended rollouts or with noisy data, producing under- or over-dispersed ensembles.
infographic.paper_title: Learning calibrated probabilistic forecasts using Koopman mode decomposition and the continuous ranked probability score

title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Hessian-Driven Nesterov Acceleration with Adam-Style Preconditioning
authors: Yaxin Yu, Long Chen, Minfu Feng
abstract: Stochastic first-order methods use sampled gradients to reduce per-iteration costs, but estimation errors can slow convergence and, in some settings, cause divergence. To improve gradient accuracy while retaining acceleration, we develop scalar and diagonal versions of VR-Adam-SHANG for smooth stochastic convex optimization. The methods combine STORM-type recursive estimation, Adam-style preconditioning, and SHANG's accelerated interpolation and correction, using at most two stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration without full-gradient refreshes. Under unbiased sampling, bounded variance, and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise, polynomial steps with prescribed initialization yield $O(1/K)$ mean-square gradient-estimation error and expected objective-gap bounds combining $O(1/K^2)$ initial-energy decay with an $O(1/\sqrt K)$ stochastic term after $K$ iterations. These guarantees require neither monotonicity of the preconditioner nor a uniform positive lower bound on its eigenvalues. The analysis also establishes polynomial-step convergence of projected nonrecursive Adam-SHANG-s, filling a gap in its original theory. Experiments compare the methods at matched sample-gradient budgets. In every tested setting, at least one of the two versions achieves the lowest mean terminal objective gap among all compared methods.

infographic.key_insight: VR-Adam-SHANG combines variance reduction, adaptive preconditioning, and acceleration to achieve expected objective-gap bounds with O(1/K²) initial-energy decay plus an O(1/√K) stochastic term.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The methods offer accelerated stochastic convex optimization with at most two sampled-gradient evaluations per iteration and no full-gradient refreshes.
method: Use STORM-type recursive estimation to reduce gradient noise.
Combine scalar or diagonal Adam-style preconditioning with SHANG acceleration and correction.
Apply prescribed initialization and polynomial step schedules to obtain O(1/K) mean-square gradient-estimation error.

infographic.watch_item: The guarantees assume smooth convex objectives, unbiased sampling, bounded variance, and mean-square smoothness of gradient noise; they do not establish performance for general nonconvex problems.
infographic.paper_title: Variance-Reduced Stochastic Hessian-Driven Nesterov Acceleration with Adam-Style Preconditioning

title: Robust Domain-Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
authors: Yankai Chen, Sida Lin, Yifan Li, Hanjun Luo, Hanrong Zhang, Zhuohan Xie
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) merges the capabilities of multiple domain-expert teachers, such as mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, into a single compact student. Since all domains share a limited training budget, how to allocate it across domains directly determines the quality of distillation. Existing methods allocate the budget by each domain's learning progress, but offer no guarantee for lagging domains. We therefore introduce distributionally robust optimization (DRO) into MOPD to prioritize the worst-performing domain. However, the per-domain training signals are estimated from a few rollouts and are inherently noisy, so directly applying DRO mistakes noise for the worst case, lets occasional spikes hijack the budget, and protects inherently hard domains rather than truly regressing ones. To address these issues, we propose RDS-MOPD, which keeps the DRO objective and redesigns its three parts: it shifts the allocation only when differences clearly exceed the noise, bounds the influence of any single anomaly, and defines the worst case as the regression from each domain's own best level, all with theoretical guarantees. Experiments show that RDS-MOPD outperforms recent competing methods and ranks first on most mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: RDS-MOPD allocates multi-teacher distillation effort toward domains regressing from their own best performance, while resisting noisy signals and isolated anomalies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach helps allocate a limited training budget across math, coding, and instruction-following teachers when building a compact student model.
method: Use distributionally robust optimization to prioritize the worst-regressing domain.
Shift domain allocation only when signal differences clearly exceed noise.
Bound individual anomalies’ influence and measure regression against each domain’s own best level.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports outperforming recent competing methods and ranking first on most math, code-generation, and instruction-following benchmarks, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance may depend on reliably estimating noise and tracking each domain’s best level from sparse rollouts.
infographic.paper_title: Robust Domain-Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation

title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
authors: Ziyuan Chen, Tong Gan, Wei Zhang, Ruofei Fang, Boyue Tang, Zhenhua Lin
abstract: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing long proof developments. We present Statopia, an ecosystem that jointly develops Statopia Prover, an independent agent specialized for formalizing and proving results in statistics and machine learning, and Statlib, a Lean~4 library built with the prover and organized for automated use. The prover controls its own execution without relying on external coding agents. It is built for formal proof discovery and checking existing proofs. A natural-language proof, when available, guides its search but is not required: from a statement alone, the prover develops the argument itself and constructs a Lean proof. Its workflow integrates source preparation, statement review, library supported planning and proof construction. Dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups support parallel, resumable proof development. Statlib's shared definitions and theorem interfaces are organized for retrieval and composition by agents, and its coverage of statistics keeps expanding. Verified results and usage feedback from the prover inform reviewed library updates, so that proof development drives this expansion. A cross-platform application provides an interactive workspace for uploading source files and running tasks locally or in the cloud.

infographic.key_insight: Statopia pairs an autonomous Lean 4 prover with an evolving statistics library to turn statements, with or without supplied proofs, into machine-checked results.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The ecosystem targets verifiable statistical and machine-learning theory through reusable formal infrastructure and parallel, resumable proof workflows.
method: Integrate source preparation, statement review, library-supported planning and Lean proof construction.
Coordinate long developments using dynamic proof dependency graphs and task groups.
Expand Statlib through reviewed updates informed by verified results and prover usage.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the architecture and workflow but reports no benchmark results, success rates or quantitative evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Machine checking validates the formal statement, so faithful reconstruction of source assumptions remains critical.
infographic.paper_title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics

title: Gradient Estimation for LLM-Embedded Simulation Optimization
authors: Ruiyang Jin, Siyang Gao
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in operational simulators to represent context-dependent human decisions, which opens new possibilities for simulation optimization. However, the LLM acts as a black box, so derivatives through its decisions are unavailable for gradient-based policy search. Finite difference estimation can avoid this requirement, but the required paired simulations that sample LLM actions independently often disagree, and such action switches persist under small perturbations, which inflates the gradient variance to order $c^{-2}$ for perturbation radius $c$. To control this variance, we develop a behavioral common random number framework. It first applies maximal coupling to the LLM's action distributions, preserving each simulation's behavioral law while making action switches as rare as possible, which reduces the variance bound to $O(c^{-1})$. It then applies first-switch conditioning, which averages over whether a switch occurs, together with an impact-aware extension that prioritizes influential switches. Under suitable stability conditions, both keep the variance bounded as $c$ shrinks. We further establish improved complexity bounds for projected stochastic approximation. Experiments on synthesized and LLM-embedded simulators confirm the theory and show substantial performance gains.

infographic.key_insight: Coordinating LLM actions across paired simulations reduces finite-difference gradient variance from O(c⁻²) to O(c⁻¹), while first-switch conditioning keeps it bounded under suitable stability conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables more reliable gradient-based policy optimization in operational simulators with black-box, LLM-driven human decisions.
method: Maximally couple LLM action distributions to minimize action switches while preserving each simulation’s behavioral law.
Condition on the first switch to average over whether it occurs and control gradient variance.
Use an impact-aware extension to prioritize influential switches.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on synthesized and LLM-embedded simulators support the variance theory and show substantial performance gains; the paper also establishes improved complexity bounds for projected stochastic approximation.
infographic.watch_item: Bounded variance requires suitable stability conditions, and implementation must support coupling the LLM action distributions.
infographic.paper_title: Gradient Estimation for LLM-Embedded Simulation Optimization
